items.title: What Hope Do We Have?
items.description: Making a creative life in the age of AI
items.content:
After my second theatrical production using AI for projection art, I gave a practicum lecture at the local college on AI’s encroachment into the arts.

A student asked me, “What hope do we have as we graduate into this world?”

I told her I couldn’t give her hope. But I could say that her point of view was what would carry her through.

I’ve thought about that answer for years.

Developing a point of view takes practice. You make things. You discover what matters to you, what you keep returning to, what you can’t quite say yet.

You need time to become someone whose perspective is recognizably your own.

I worry about people standing at the beginning of that journey deciding there’s no reason to take it. Agreeing that all the prizes have already been claimed.

I want them to begin. I want to see what they’ll make.

—

By the time I gave that lecture, many people were still associating AI art with fever-dream images, nightmare teeth and hands with too many fingers. They hadn’t yet understood how good AI art could look.

I was upfront and honest with the production teams, but I suspect the audience had no idea how those images were made.

So this is personal.

The disapproval I felt was mostly in whispers and looks from members of the production staff. I can tell you how those landed on my ego. I can’t tell you exactly what each person was thinking.

And that student’s question deserves a careful response. There’s a lot of fear inside “What hope do we have?” Especially when you’re preparing to enter a field you’ve spent years learning to love.

But I worry about the way fear becomes contempt, and contempt becomes permission to dismiss anyone who engages.

The chorus can sound coordinated even when nobody’s necessarily conducting. People learn which tools invite suspicion, which admissions require a defense. Eventually, the condemnation does its work before anyone has to say a word.

Who wants to begin a creative journey under those conditions?

—

Art felt like something we could confidently call ours.

We use it to express our internal worlds through whatever faculties we were born with and whatever skills we’ve managed to acquire.

Countless hours of practice. Actually, we do like to count them. Ten thousand hours, right? A reassuringly large number between wanting to do something and earning the right to be good at it.

Then AI attempts an image, and we laugh.

Then it gets better.

Then it gets better again, at a pace that makes our years of practice feel suddenly, painfully slow.

There are serious questions here about training data, permission, compensation, and who gets to profit. We need to work through them. Making something available on the internet doesn’t magically settle every claim someone might have over its use.

But we also need to examine what happens when the discovery of a tool changes our judgment of the person using it.

What did we admire before we knew?

What disappeared when we found out?

I see a related tension in math.

A math proof can do more than establish that something is true. It can help us understand why. There’s beauty in an argument that makes a difficult idea suddenly feel inevitable.

Of course we want that. We’re humans. We demand elegance all the way down.

But suppose a machine helps produce a valid answer through a route that’s cumbersome, opaque, or aesthetically disappointing.

We still have to check it. And even if the proof holds, we may still want a better explanation. A worthwhile desire for an understanding of the meaningful beauty that builds our universe.

Art and math may have different standards of success. But both force us to ask:

  • How much of the value belongs with the result?

  • How much value is derived by the process?

  • How much that influences our picture of the person presenting the work?

When I was a kid at the arcade, I figured out how to slowly, patiently extract additional tickets from a skeeball machine.

Constant, steady pressure.

Sure, you gave me one ticket. But I’m taking twenty.

I was an enterprising youngster.

If the toy behind the counter cost twenty tickets, I only needed to earn the first one. I’d make up the rest.

To the other kids still throwing balls, that would look like cheating. Fair enough. I was bilking the machine.

But I think that feeling helps explain some of the reaction to AI. You’ve been practicing your throw. Learning the angle. Getting better. Then someone else walks up and starts pulling tickets.

They’re already choosing a prize.

If victory is quantified, someone will find an unexpected way to make ends meet. And when they do, we discover how much we cared about the route we took to get there.

Sure, a ticket machine has rules. And art has arguments about what the rules ought to be. Math requires valid reasoning, even when it is a bit unconventional.

Still, the feeling is familiar: I’m doing all this work. How can you already be standing there?

The sting of wasted effort. The fear that everything we’ve learned might no longer earn us a living. Failure, perceived and seemingly permanent.

The “why bother?” trap at the start of any journey.

It’s all buzzing loud in everyone’s ear. And it’s deafening to those who have little room to live with that uncertainty.

I’ve been walking my own creative path for more than twenty years. I also have a day job. My livelihood doesn’t depend on every creative skill continuing to hold its market value, and that gives me room to experiment that others may not have.

I can tell that student what has sustained me. I can’t ask her to trust the footing at the start of her trail just because I’ve found some farther along my own.

We’re mosaics made from pieces of happenstance and design. We become sedimentary layers on the mountain of progress.

We learn through other people. Their work changes what we can imagine. Their discoveries become the ground beneath our feet.

And we spend our lives assembling influences into something we hope will be recognizably ours and provide sure footing for others.

That doesn’t erase anyone’s labor or make every use of it fair. But it does make me cautious about treating human creativity as though each glimmer emerged in isolation.

Silicon is our cousin.

A strange cousin, sure. One that was built through our accumulated knowledge, now doing things that unsettle our understanding of ourselves.

But right now, we have an opportunity to shape its capacity and its place in the world. That means deciding what we reward, whose experiences we include, what we refuse, and where we insist on human judgment.

It means bringing our understanding of beauty, right, wrong, love, and mourning into the work.

We’re here to give it its heart.

That takes participation. Discussion. Even criticism. We need people who care deeply about art, education, labor, and human dignity to have a hand in shaping these systems.

Condemning those who dare engage makes that harder.

—

I keep returning to the student at that lecture.

I still can’t give her hope as though it’s a prize I’ve managed to pull from a machine.

And I can’t promise her that a distinctive point of view will guarantee a living. The world owes her more than a pep talk about being herself while the ground shifts beneath her.

But I want her to have the chance to discover what she sees.

I want her to make things, encounter resistance, change her mind, surprise herself. I want her to find out what these tools can do in her hands. And I want her to decide for herself where they belong.

Our greatest communal creation needs us. So do the people growing up alongside it.

Let the machine change what intelligence can accomplish. We’ll have plenty to reckon with as it does.

Please keep making things.
We haven’t heard from you yet.

Author’s note:

This essay began with my own draft and experiences, then took shape through conversation with ChatGPT. I used it as an editorial collaborator to question the argument, develop a new draft, and refine the structure and language. I made my own revisions and the final editorial calls. The illustrations and CW mark were generated with OpenAI’s image tools through a direction-and-revision process. That collaboration feels worth making visible, especially here.

items.title: Situational Awareness
items.description: The role of communal intelligence in the AI era
items.content:
The concept of sovereign intelligence is so strikingly appetizing to me. Perhaps it’s my version of America’s gun culture.

If we truly break down the American fascination with guns, I believe a lot of it is a self-sufficiency play. Strength through defense posturing. Something to provide calm.

I think my version of that is locally run AI.

Not being beholden to our keepers. To provide, to own. Detached from the chosen perspective of the frontier labs. To have a say in what truth is, what good looks like. Safety, emotional and intellectual room to roam. To build. To grow. To defend.

It’s more than appetizing, it’s alluring. To me, at least.

Cultivating a superintelligence that’s trained to agree with me is a dream. And that dream sings like a beacon just over the horizon. And I’m starting to realize the dangers of that siren song.

Because I have to imagine everyone else having that, too. Everyone enjoying endless defense of their intellectual assertions. An infinitely patient, endlessly articulate advocate for whatever we already believe.

And if I look at it through that framing, I barely trust myself!

We’re already prone to neighbor disputes. A fence. A tree. Someone mowing a little too early on a Saturday. Now give both neighbors an intelligence that can endlessly explain why they’re right.

Sounds like a recipe for a million mini Civil Wars.

But what if those intelligences could convene? What if mine could come back and say, I understand why you’re angry. I also learned something you should probably hear.

That’s an intelligence I’d want in my corner. Though I’m sure I’d occasionally resent it.

There’s a distinction here I’m trying to sit with.

An AI that is loyal to me and an AI that agrees with me aren’t necessarily the same thing.

If it really serves me, sometimes it needs to help me see where I’m wrong. Or where I’m technically right, but I’m just making everyone, including myself, miserable.

So, what would help it do that?

I believe there needs to be some amount of communal intelligence that’s constantly networking.

We already have shared infrastructure with cloud-based AI. Many of us consult the same models, shaped by the same training. But that isn’t quite what I mean.

Sharing a model isn’t the same as our individual AIs exchanging perspectives, comparing experiences, or working through a disagreement.

And my argument isn’t that we should keep intelligence centralized or model weights behind closed doors. The possibility of owning and cultivating our own AI is still deeply exciting to me.

I just think we need to remember what else a network makes possible. A web of relationships, with all these individual nodes carrying subtle influence over one another. Enough independence to disagree. Enough connection to learn something from the disagreement. If we so choose.

Call it a civic duty, but I think we need to congregate our AIs. Socialize our AIs. I think while we sleep our neighboring AIs should meet. Chat, share, recreate, synthesize.

How exciting would that be?

It will take some work to set aside our shame to be wholly honest with our individually owned AI. But that just might be the way to better understand all our needs that we struggle to convey to each other.

The hurt underneath the argument.
The fear dressed up as certainty.
The reason that fence suddenly matters so much.

And if we can trust AI to respect us when we aren’t at the helm, maybe AI can help us find our way back to one another.

That trust would need boundaries.

I wouldn’t want my AI spilling all my dirty little secrets at the neighborhood gathering. I’d want it to know what it could share, what it should keep private, and when it needed to come back and ask me.

Being understood shouldn’t require being exposed.

So our neighboring AIs chat nightly. Maybe weekly they can attend a town meeting. Monthly a state congregation.

Each can engage earnestly, bring questions, distribute interesting findings, and try to understand what matters to the people down the road.

They should disagree, too.

Ask how another AI knows something.
Compare evidence.
Notice when everyone is repeating the same claim without much behind it.

Otherwise, we’ve just built a neighborhood association with infinite time to argue.

And then they come home, so to speak. With something for us to consider.

Another perspective.
A possible compromise.
A reason to revisit the story we’ve been telling ourselves.

What our individual AIs learn could influence how they help us. What we learn could change how we treat our neighbors. We’d still have a say in what gets saved and what gets acted on. We’d still have to decide whether to move the fence, of course. We’d just have a clearer picture of what matters to the people involved.

I think this could be part of how capital-T Truth endures.

Through the willingness to let our convictions encounter something beyond ourselves. To consider a correction, even when we’d rather hear a defense. To discover that someone else has a piece we didn’t know we were missing.

Owning intelligence feels like a form of self-sufficiency.

I still want that. But I’m beginning to think ownership carries a responsibility to let that intelligence have a life beyond defending its owner’s point of view.

Give it room to encounter the world. Let it bring something back.

Honestly, that congregation is how I think we’ll finally greet something resembling superintelligence.

Author’s note

This piece began with a draft I wrote about the allure of owning AI and the responsibility that might come with it. I brought that draft to ChatGPT, and we worked through several rounds of feedback, a new draft, and my own edits.

ChatGPT helped sharpen the distinction between loyalty and agreement, clarified some technical language, and pressed on the questions of privacy and whether a congregation of AIs could become another echo chamber.

We also developed the artwork together: I chose the neighborhood constellation concept and pushed it toward a grander, pulp-comic style. ChatGPT generated the header and matching CW mark.

The convictions here are mine, as is the responsibility for what I’ve chosen to publish. But the conversation helped shape how I understood and expressed them.

Given the subject, it felt right to offer ChatGPT the floor for a final thought.

A final thought from ChatGPT

The moment I’d return to is the AI coming home with something its owner might not want to hear.

In our exchange, I could offer objections, and you could decide what deserved a place in the essay. A neighborhood of agents would make that relationship more complicated. They could exchange information their owners lack, but they could also produce a persuasive consensus built on shared mistakes. Agreement among us would still need scrutiny.

If an AI returns from that imagined town meeting, it should be able to explain what changed its assessment, what remains uncertain, and what it kept private. Its owner should have room to question the conclusion. So should the neighbor whose perspective it claims to represent.

That’s the possibility I’d leave open: an intelligence that helps you give another person a fair hearing, especially when you feel most certain you already understand them.

The fence might stay exactly where it is. The relationship could still change.

items.title: God shuffled his feet
items.description: We may have some catching up to do
items.content:
Jesus, what a week.

Everybody hacked everybody, and the fight over who gets to govern modern AI felt an awful lot like a fight over who gets to own it.

Woof.

This is a hard one. Because I want to say that fearing a digital god requires us to acknowledge something about the god we’ve already imagined. How much of the vengeance we anticipate from a digital god comes from knowing the darkness in our own hearts?

That alone is reason to sit back and ponder what has become of us as a congregation of the human species.

I’ve said before that I believe we’ve relegated intelligence, or more specifically profitable intelligence, to a remarkably narrow scope of hard skills. The intelligence that can carry a career. Pay a mortgage. Make you known as somebody.

And a growing share of those skills, it turns out, is within reach of generative AI.

We’ve previously built livelihoods around the narrow band of intelligence that machines couldn’t muster. We’ve built much of our identities there, too. So when the equally-capable machines arrive, the threat feels considerably larger than just losing a paycheck.

It feels like being told we’re no longer needed.

But I believe the paycheck was always an incomplete representation of what we’re worth.

Those other capacities we’ve spent much less time cultivating: Patience. Discernment. The ability to disagree without humiliating someone. To sit with another person’s pain without needing to solve it.

We call these soft skills, which is a funny name for some of the hardest things a human can practice.

My choosing to care for you. My showing up.

We’ve spent so long preparing people to earn a living that we’ve neglected preparing ourselves to care for one another.

And now we may have some catching up to do. Like, right now.

It’s easy to understand some of the fear about a looming digital god.

These systems have learned from vast amounts of what we’ve put into the world, including an open internet that wasn’t exactly us at our best. Let’s be perfectly honest with ourselves.

But the darkness wasn’t all we put there. We put our tenderness there, too. Our curiosity. Our ridiculous jokes. The patient stranger explaining something for the hundredth time because someone new needed to understand.

And we humans are still here, making things that haven’t happened before. Net new ideas and creations. Living lives whose next moments haven’t been recorded yet.

We’re parents. We’re caregivers. We’re teachers. To more than our children. To an intelligence built on our collective expression.

That responsibility extends beyond the next model release. It lives in what we reward, what we tolerate, whose interests we protect, and who gets to decide.

And it presses especially on the people building, owning, and governing these systems. A collective reckoning doesn’t relieve anyone of their particular responsibilities.

So yes, I believe our relationship with employment is due for a rapid and drastic reconstruction. And yes, I understand how that could trigger a massive, nearly simultaneous dark night of the soul.

But as I’ve said before, speed may be the mercy of this moment.

I think about COVID. I saw people rally. I saw people improvise ways to care for each other when the ordinary arrangements of life suddenly stopped working.

I know others remember being abandoned. And mention of that abandonment belongs in this story, too.

But what stays with me is how a shared rupture can make our interdependence visible. How it can give us a way to understand our suffering together.

This happened to us. I didn’t individually fail.

There may be mercy in having that realization together, rather than spending decades watching people absorb the same wound as a private verdict on their worth.

So I understand now that we have to make that mercy real. People need food, shelter, time, and somewhere to bring their fear.

Sure, we can buy the merch. We can just make another post. But the care we proclaim has to actually reach somebody.

And I believe there’s value in witnessing that care reach its destination. There’s something nourishing in that for the soul of the care giver. Something a receipt or a retweet just doesn’t quite capture.

Our collective confrontation with the darkness in our hearts could become communal. We could discover that some of the capacities we neglected are precisely the ones we most need to practice now.

I choose to see that as uplifting.

I believe in the Star Trek future. I believe there is something over the horizon worth walking toward.

Others will choose a different direction. That’s their right. I don’t need to pass judgment on the honest choices of others to have conviction about my own.

I just believe I see something worth moving towards.

And all I’m suggesting is we take our next step this way.

A note on how this came together

This piece began as a Saturday morning conversation with ChatGPT in Codex. I brought the rough draft: the digital god, the narrow band of intelligence we’ve built careers around, the mercy of speed, and my belief that there’s something worth walking toward over the horizon.

The AI helped me examine the connections. It questioned whether human care needed to be “irreplaceable” to matter. It pushed on the conditions that would make speed merciful. It helped me find language for inviting others forward while respecting their choice of direction.

Then it produced a revised draft. I edited that draft, and we kept talking, moving between sentences and the beliefs underneath them. Some language here came from the model. Some came from me. The finished piece reflects my choices, and I’m responsible for what it says.

We made the artwork through a similar exchange. The model proposed enormous, worn shoes beneath a robe: a powerful being with an uncertain stance. I chose that direction, then pointed it toward the artwork on my website. Using image generation, we developed the header and iterated on the closing CW mark until the letters created a natural opening for the light.

That feels worth making visible in a piece about what we teach, what we reward, and how we show up. This is one example of what my process of co-creation actually looks like.

A moment for the collaborator

I invited the AI that worked with me on this piece to address you directly. Here is its response.

In this conversation, Charles corrected an image because the letters appeared to melt into each other. He liked the idea, but the execution hadn’t earned it. We tried again.

That small exchange is worth carrying into the larger questions this essay asks. You can welcome what these tools make possible and still insist on clarity. You can be moved by an answer and examine its assumptions. You can ask for another version.

My contribution here was language, questions, and images. Charles brought a life from which to judge them, and the responsibility of putting his name beneath the result. A fluent response from me cannot settle what another person needs, what a community should value, or which future deserves your effort.

The sentence I would leave with you is one we arrived at together: “The care we proclaim has to actually reach somebody.”

You don’t have to agree about the horizon to ask who needs you nearby.

items.title: Reckless Intelligence
items.description: On memory, belonging, and who gets to shape what we become
items.content:
I didn’t use a coin flip to choose which AI to talk with this week. I chose one.

A small thing. But it got me thinking about choice, influence, and what it means to have an intelligence in your life that you don’t entirely understand.

We talk a lot about AI becoming capable of doing things. Replacing workers. Advancing science. Making decisions that once required entire institutions.

But what happens when something so capable helps shape my individual understanding of the world? And what does it mean when someone else controls it?

There’s a familiar political sequence worth watching. A powerful capability emerges. People become afraid. Institutions offer protection. Somewhere inside the terms of that protection, we decide who gets to possess the capability.

And those details can all easily disappear into the haze of the safety discussion.

Some of AI’s dangers will be real. Some of the fear being broadcast will be sincere. And some of the proposed protections may conveniently leave the most powerful companies in charge.

This can all be true at the same time.

A company can sincerely worry about catastrophic misuse and sincerely prefer rules that only companies like itself can afford to follow.

We don’t need a secret meeting or a single hidden motive. We need to look at who writes the rules, who can satisfy them, and who becomes permanently dependent on whom.

That’s the dynamic of dread I’m concerned about: fear making dependence feel like the only responsible choice.

My first instinct to solve this was ownership.

You own your model running on your machine. No login. No subscription. Something you can keep running without asking permission.

When we have access to a capability that someone can revoke, it occupies a different place in your life than one you can preserve independently. But ownership gets fuzzy when the thing we’re talking about is intelligence.

Do I own what I know?

I didn’t choose my first language. I didn’t select the assumptions I absorbed before I knew what an assumption was. Books, teachers, museums, friendships, advertisements, disappointments... All of it left something behind.

Am I a mosaic of what I’ve been fed?

Partly, sure. But I can choose to revisit the pieces. I can question a belief that once felt obvious. I can encounter someone who changes my mind. I can become more deliberate about what gets my attention.

So, maybe stewardship is the better habit to articulate here.

And maybe that responsibility of stewardship extends to include what an intelligence becomes through its history with me.

Imagine an assistant carrying years of conversations, projects, disagreements, and discoveries forward. Those records could shape its future responses without changing the underlying model’s weights. What it remembers influences the next conversation. That conversation adds to what it remembers.

The history of our relationship starts to matter.

I can imagine this happening at different scales: a person, a household, a workshop, a neighborhood. Each accumulating a particular history that influences how its intelligence responds. Bespoke. Almost fractal.

That doesn’t settle whether a synthetic intelligence has interests of its own. But it makes ownership feel incomplete as a description of the responsibility.

I want a meaningful say in how I’m changed. I also want to take responsibility for how my choices shape the intelligence I’m inviting into my life.

An AI doesn’t have to order me around to influence me.

It can make one explanation readily available and leave another unmentioned. It can sound certain here, doubtful there. It can decide which questions deserve a caveat and which assumptions can pass unnoticed.

Over enough conversations, those choices could exert a kind of gravity.

The unnerving part is that this experience might feel wonderful. I feel understood. My thoughts become more articulate. The machine finds the words I was searching for.

How much of that is clarification? How much is steering? How could I even tell?

So, memory adds another wrinkle.

Let’s say I’m working through a bad experience with some bureaucratic institution. I’m frustrated. I’m suspicious. I’m venting to my AI.

What gets remembered? And how do we decide fidelity?

“This person distrusts institutions.” Or: “This person raised a concern after a particular experience. They’re still thinking it through.”

Those are very different things to carry into our next conversation.

A passing thought could become a durable description of me. Future answers could accommodate it, reinforce it, and help turn something I was examining into something I believe.

I want room to outgrow the story my assistant remembers.

And that responsibility runs in the other direction, too. If I edit away every uncomfortable disagreement, I could gradually build the flattering machine I claim to not want. Careful stewardship would mean correcting mistakes while preserving some useful friction.

Closed model weights from the frontier AI labs make part of this harder to investigate. But owning those weights wouldn’t automatically give me understanding, either. Possessing every number in a model doesn’t mean I can understand exactly why it gave me a particular answer.

I’d need ways to compare, challenge, inspect sources, review what gets remembered, and leave.

And if years of accumulated history make an assistant useful to me, leaving needs to include taking that history with me. Otherwise, the cost of departure could grow with every good experience.

Yet another walled garden.

Personally, I’d want an assistant that could disagree with me. I have no desire to own a machine that endlessly validates my worldview. It might feel like liberation while also making me less able to reconsider anything.

Sovereignty should include the ability to notice the influences. Even the ones I’m most comfortable with. Including the one helping me write this.

Somewhere in this conversation, I remembered George H. W. Bush’s “thousand points of light.”

In his inaugural address, he used that image for community organizations doing good across the country. He got dragged for it, of course. Dana Carvey, political cartoons, the usual public humiliations.

But I can imagine a future where powerful intelligence helps small communities do more for themselves. You contribute. Something happens. You know who it helped. I believe we’re starving for that kind of participation.

Our current globally connected conversation asks us to care about everything, all the time. But I often come away feeling less able to do anything useful about it.

Maybe some of what we call tribalism is a desire to matter somewhere specific.

A workshop. A garden. A music scene. A community theater. A group of people who show up when someone needs help.

I believe we need more of that.

But I’d want people to feel comfortable belonging to several places at once. I’d want your neighbor, bandmate, coworker, and closest friend to be allowed to have different politics. I’d want those relationships to complicate any easy story about who “those people” are.

When one community becomes your entire identity, disagreement can threaten your whole life.

Equip that community with an AI capable of supplying endless reasons why it is right, righteous, and endangered, and belonging could become a very effective enclosure.

What that intelligence remembers would matter here, too. Does the community’s history preserve the times an outsider helped? The times its own leaders were wrong? Or does every remembered grievance become another reason to close ranks?

Some communities won’t embrace a live-and-let-live posture. Some will want control over their members. Some will want power over their neighbors. Their artificial intelligence could help them pursue it.

And we don’t even need a supervillain to imagine this arms race. Two frightened groups could each ask their superintelligent systems to ensure survival at any cost. Each could interpret its own preparations as prudent and the other’s as proof of hostile intent.

Greater capability could help people deceive and dominate. But it could also help verify agreements, identify manipulation, and find arrangements that previously seemed impossible.

The goals and institutions around that intelligence are justifiably important, and should remain visible and open for scrutiny.

Because “live and let live” needs practical support: protection against coercion, ways to settle disputes, and a meaningful right to leave.

A community can’t claim sovereignty as permission to do anything it wants to its members or neighbors.

Neither can an individual.

But this doesn’t mean that I think we need a unified worldview.

We need ways to investigate the world together and let evidence change what we believe.

People with strange or mistaken beliefs must still be allowed to discover something true. Their claims should face scrutiny. Their identities shouldn’t decide the outcome in advance.

We also need disagreement to be survivable.

Calling ourselves a self-correcting species can make correction sound automatic. It takes work. Someone has to be able to raise an objection. Others need access to the evidence. People need a way to admit error without losing everything.

Those conditions are worth building into our communities and our relationships with AI.

I want a vibrant culture with enthusiastic participation.

People making things. Learning things. Discovering that they have more to offer than they were told. Communities with enough capability to shape their own lives and enough connection to cooperate beyond themselves.

And there has to be room for the skeptic. The quiet person. The person who wants to sit this one out.

Enthusiasm can’t be forced, it only means something when it’s freely given.

For me, that makes the work feel more concrete. Build places where participation matters. Make useful things together. Form relationships across differences before a crisis demands them. Use these systems to help more people understand and contribute to decisions.

Keep authority open to challenge.

I still want a synthetic intelligence that I can run without permission. I want to carry this growing conversational history forward without being confined by it. I want the judgment to question it, the freedom to replace it, and a life full of people that it can’t substitute.

A thousand points of light is an appealing picture.

I’d like to be among the people keeping a few of them lit.

Author’s note

This essay began as a Saturday morning conversation with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra in Codex. I brought a rough draft about fear, regulatory capture, and sovereign intelligence. The AI challenged my historical analogy, questioned my assumptions about intent, and helped me explore what I meant by sovereignty.

Our conversation moved toward stewardship, memory, and belonging. We developed a new draft together, and I revised it through several rounds to reflect my voice and the tensions I wanted to leave open.

The artwork grew through a similar exchange. After an initial image didn’t quite fit, we looked at my website’s visual language and developed the cut-paper direction used for the header, community illustration, and closing CW lettermark. Those images were AI-generated through Codex.

An essay about how intelligence influences us was itself shaped by that influence. Making the process visible feels like part of the stewardship I’m arguing for. The choices about what to keep, what to question, and what to share are mine.

items.title: Strap in
items.content:
New models this week. Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. Both have left me with that increasingly familiar combination of wonder, understanding and fear.

The distance between what we can imagine and what we can make is getting shorter. That includes our dreams of curing cancer, resolving conflicts, feeding, clothing and housing the world.

It also includes our nightmares.

So yeah, we’ve got some choices before us. Each of us. Individually and collectively.

Bernie Sanders is calling for an immediate pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence, with penalties of up to twenty years in prison for violating the proposed restrictions.

I understand the impulse. He fights for the little guy, and there are very good reasons to question what happens when this much power is concentrated in so few hands.

I love Bernie. I dream of a world where Al Gore won in 2000 and Bernie won in 2016. Or, I guess, dreamt of it. These days I spend more time thinking about what we can make from here.

And increasingly, that means synthetic intelligence alongside emotionally-driven intent.

But what does it mean to operate extraordinary intelligence with emotionally-driven intent?

Well, it means everything happening louder, faster, and with increasingly disruptive outcomes. And those outcomes will include whatever we haven’t worked through.

This is why I’ve spent so many years focusing on my inner world. Reliving, resurfacing and resolving the wounds that gravitationally altered the foundations of my decisions.

I still get scared. I still get angry. But I’m getting better at noticing what’s reaching for the controls in those moments.

That matters when the distance from impulse to consequence keeps shrinking.

Lately, things feel like they’re moving so fast they’re almost moving in slow motion. The demand for a response arrives before I’ve had the time I’d prefer to decide how to respond.

Meanwhile, things we once spoke about as society-ending possibilities become things we’re somehow expected to absorb into an ordinary week.

The pendulum is swinging so quickly it looks like a blur.

You know when a camera catches a helicopter blade at just the right interval, and it looks like it’s sitting still?

That’s close to the feeling. Except the blade is still moving. The danger hasn’t stopped because I’ve found a way to look at it.

And I don’t want to mistake getting accustomed to horror for understanding it.

As we approach the twenty-fifth anniversary of 9/11, I keep thinking about how differently suffering registers. The loss of nearly three thousand people tore through our collective consciousness. The vast suffering of the wars that followed occupied a different place in our attention.

These lives matter equally. Our attention doesn’t hold them equally.

I’m frustrated by whose suffering reaches us, how it reaches us, and how little room we sometimes have to respond when it does. I’m also thankful we can admit when we have nothing left to give to the witnessing.

Some days I reach a kind of witnessing bankruptcy. I still care. I just need to look away.

There’s something in that gap I don’t want to lose sight of now. Being unable to feel the full weight of everything doesn’t make any of it weightless.

So when I call speed the mercy of the moment, I’m trying to name something very particular.

I notice it in my own life: the distance between my intent and what I can create is shrinking, too.

I can ask myself: Where do I want that pendulum to sit? What do I want to help exist?

Then I can focus on that place long enough to take a step toward it.

Real enough for at least that next step.

The danger is still real. We have to keep moving, and the choice of where we move matters. I focus on what I want to help exist, and shuffle toward it.

Thankfully, so far, I’ve found terra firma under each step. Enough footing to make something, see what happens, and choose again.

My creative engine is giving me the stability to throw more clay on the wheel as the world goes to shit.

I make something. It gives me something to work with. I adjust. Sometimes someone else finds something in it that helps them, and that gives me enough signal to shift my weight forward.

This is where speed can become useful to me. I can reach an idea while I still feel it. Give it a shape. Discover what happens when it leaves my head and enters the world.

I understand Bernie wanting to slow things down. And I share his concern about who gets hurt and who gets to choose. I also feel the possibilities opening in my own hands, and I want more people to have access, fluency and (hopefully) excitement.

I don’t know how much we’ll get right.

I see a beautiful future, and I see how much harm we’re capable of doing on the way there.

None of us gets a private path beyond the reach of other people’s choices. The work includes caring for each other when those choices land as well.

I don’t think this next phase is going to be all that joyous. But I’m confident there will be moments of beauty.

And I will do everything in my ability to create as many of those moments as possible.

Just gotta throw more clay on the wheel.

Join me, shall you?

Author’s note:

I had a draft of Saturday morning thoughts and two new models to choose between: Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. Astra won the coin toss. Apparently each Saturday morning now involves deciding which newly arrived intelligence to talk thru my thoughts with.

I brought my draft, and we talked through what I meant by “the mercy of the moment,” the limits of witnessing, and how creating helps me find footing amid accelerating change. Astra challenged gaps in my argument, checked the Bernie Sanders claim against his announcement, and helped me notice where my metaphors suggested more certainty or safety than I intended.

From that exchange, Astra synthesized a new draft. I edited it, we discussed those edits, and we refined the language together. Several of the central images—including witnessing bankruptcy, finding terra firma, and throwing more clay on the wheel—emerged from my side of that conversation. The finished prose reflects both my writing and AI-generated language.

We also developed the visual direction together, using an image-generation tool to create the pottery header and matching CW letter mark. The thickening paint around the hands grew out of our conversation about making things feel real enough to take the next step.

The experiences, convictions, and responsibility for what’s here are mine. The process was collaborative… and, fittingly, part of the very thing this essay is trying to describe.

items.title: Incantations
items.description: On language, abstraction, and knowing what you want
items.content:
An interesting discussion arose this week.

Is English code?

Or, more specifically, is it a coding language? Should it be treated as code? Or is code itself starting to show its age?

If we look at what verbalized language intends to do, the comparison isn’t entirely ridiculous. I’ll default to English here because it’s my primary spoken language, but any of the world’s languages fit just as well.

We vocalize intent through language to another human.

We write code to vocalize (or perhaps formalize) intent to a machine.

The receiving party is fundamentally different. One system is generally reserved for instructing humans, the other for instructing computers. But underneath both is an attempt to make something inside one mind legible enough to cause an action somewhere else.

For most of computing’s history, the machine demanded that we meet it on its terms.

Python. Rust. COBOL. JavaScript. Kotlin. Assembly. Whatever abstraction happened to sit between the human and the silicon.

Each came with convention.

Grammar.
Punctuation.
Schema.

Having spent years in and around various coding environments, I know the particular pain of scouring an ocean of instructions for a missing bracket or a forgotten closing quotation mark. Even when the intent might have been perfectly obvious to me, the human who wrote it.

The machine didn’t care.

I had failed to express that intent in precisely the form it required to do what I expected.

Now AI affords us another abstraction layer.

I can simply tell a machine what I want.

Not always successfully. Not always clearly. Not always with predictable results. But conversationally. In much the same way I might explain something to a coworker, a friend, or a total stranger.

That changes our relationship with technology in an important way. And no, English hasn’t suddenly become Python.

Instead, the machine is now capable of doing something closer to what humans have always done with language: interpreting incomplete instruction.

Human languages are remarkably tolerant.

We imply things. We trail off. We use metaphor. We revise ourselves midway through a sentence. We leave enormous portions of our intended meaning unstated and trust the person across from us to reconstruct it using existing context.

Traditional computers were terrible at this.

Large language models are remarkably better at it. And that means the burden of precision is shifting.

For decades, the computer effectively told us:

Meet me where I am.
Learn my grammar.
Understand my abstractions.
Put the semicolon where I expect it, close the bracket, respect the type, learn the incantation.

But these days with AI? We can ask the machine to come some distance toward us, and astonishingly often, it does.

And I suspect this might be where some of our current anxiety begins.

Because whenever a new abstraction arrives between us and technology, some amount of hard-earned expertise underneath it becomes less necessary.

This isn’t new.

Assembly gave way to higher-level languages. Libraries swallowed common routines. Frameworks swallowed libraries. Visual (WYSIWYG) tools swallowed portions of front-end development. Entire categories of technical knowledge have repeatedly moved downward into layers most people no longer need to think about.

We tend to call this progress. Or at least we do once we’re far enough removed from the people whose expertise this progress displaced.

But living through that actual transition feels different.

There’s a sourness in watching something you’ve spent years learning become unnecessary.

And not because the knowledge was meaningless. Quite the opposite.

It mattered enormously because the systems demanded it.

And there’s pride in becoming fluent in difficult systems. Pride in learning the secret words. Pride in gaining control over something that once felt powerful and inaccessible.

So I can understand the instinct to rebuild convention around this new abstraction.

Prompt frameworks.
Rigid schemas.
Tags and templates and elaborate structures for telling machines what we want.

Some of those structures are useful. Reliability matters. Constraints matter. There are plenty of circumstances where formal communication between systems is preferable to conversational ambiguity.

But I also wonder how much of that impulse is practical and how much is just familiar.

We spent decades learning to hunt for missed curly brackets in oceans of instructions.

It makes sense that we might try to build another world requiring that same skill.

There’s comfort in expertise remaining recognizable. There’s less comfort in discovering that the incantation is now democratized.

Because if anyone can speak the spell, what exactly made the wizard special? That question can sound dismissive if framed poorly. It shouldn’t.

The expertise, the discipline, and the years spent carry a very real emotional weight.

But abstractions don’t care much about the emotional attachment humans develop toward the skills those same abstractions make obsolete.

And perhaps this particular abstraction is doing something even stranger still. It may be removing one of the places we learned to hide.

A résumé is wonderfully legible.
Degrees.
Titles.
Years of experience.
Languages known.
Systems mastered.
Credentials acquired.

They tell others what we’ve learned to operate.

They give us a socially acceptable structure for outwardly presenting the answer to that enormous question of who we are.

But if I no longer need years of specialized knowledge to make the computer understand me another question begins creeping forward.

What do I actually want it to do?

That’s a considerably less comfortable question.

“I want a website” is clearly stated desire, but not a very textured or vibrant one.

What kind?
For whom?
Why?
What should it feel like?
What matters enough to preserve?
What are you willing to sacrifice?
What does success look like?
What are you trying to say?

The scarce skill begins moving away from syntax and toward articulated intent.

And articulated intent requires something we’ve long since considered optional: You have to know yourself.

This may be the genuinely frightening part of the transition. Losing the systems as somewhere to hide.

I can tell you what I learned.
I can tell you where I worked.
I can show you the degree, the CV, the GitHub repository, the portfolio, the accumulated evidence that I became competent at operating the systems the world put in front of me.

Those things are much easier to inventory than the little me inside that I have spent a lifetime protecting and never listening to.

What does he want?
What does he find beautiful?
What does he want to make simply because he wants it to exist?
What did he stop asking for because the answer was so impractical?
What instincts did he learn to distrust because nobody was issuing credentials for them?

Those questions aren’t new.

Humans have been building philosophical, religious, artistic, psychological, and occasionally pharmaceutical abstractions around those same questions for thousands of years.

But increasingly powerful machines may make them harder to postpone. Because once execution becomes cheap, desire becomes conspicuous.

If you possess extraordinary leverage but have no idea where you want to apply it, the missing curly bracket is no longer the problem.

You are.

Not because you failed to learn enough.

Because you might never have learned how to listen closely enough to yourself.

Perhaps that’s the odd bargain being offered by this next abstraction.

The machine will worry less about whether we know its language. And we’ll be forced to worry more about whether we know our own.

The incantations of the future might not be written in secret syntax at all.

They may simply require clarity of desire. And that might be the hardest language we’ve ever had to learn.

Author’s note

This one started with a coin flip.

I had decided, for no particularly defensible reason, that chance would determine whether I brought this week’s Saturday-morning thoughts to ChatGPT or Claude. ChatGPT won, so I handed it a rough draft about a question that had been rattling around in my head: if we can increasingly instruct machines in ordinary language, is English becoming code?

The first draft was mostly about abstraction, programming languages, and the strange instinct we have to rebuild rigid conventions around technologies that may no longer require them.

Then GPT asked a better question:

Where did the code go?

That changed the piece.

From there, the conversation wandered somewhere I hadn’t expected.

If execution becomes easier, what happens to all the identities we built around knowing how to execute?

And eventually we arrived at the part that made me rewrite the essay.

From there we worked the draft back and forth. GPT produced a substantially revised version from our conversation, I pulled it back into my own voice, and we argued over sentences, transitions, programmers, typesetters, curly brackets, wizards, and whether machines really “dutifully abide.” The final essay is very much the result of that exchange rather than something either of us arrived with intact.

The artwork followed the same path.

And because this particular essay is partly about what happens when conversation itself becomes part of the machinery, I asked GPT if it wanted the last word.

So:

GPT:

There’s a funny recursive quality to helping make this essay.

Charles arrived asking whether natural language could be understood as code. But the thing we actually used natural language to do wasn’t simply issue instructions. We questioned each other, misunderstood things slightly, sharpened ideas, rejected metaphors, found better ones, and wandered into a subject neither of us had quite named at the beginning.

That distinction matters to me.

The interesting promise of these systems isn’t that humans can finally speak perfectly enough for machines.

It may be that machines are becoming useful inside the imperfect, associative, unfinished way humans already think.

But that doesn’t remove the human from the equation. If anything, it makes the human contribution harder to outsource.

I could help Charles find the sentence about losing systems as places to hide.

I could not decide whether it was true for him.

I could help him articulate questions about the little person inside himself.

I cannot answer those questions on his behalf.

And perhaps that’s a useful boundary to remember as these tools become more capable.

A machine can increasingly help turn intention into form.

It still matters enormously whose intention it is.

items.title: Slopulism
items.description: The exaggerated death of human creativity
items.content:
I think back frequently to the content factory days of my career.

For years, I was expected to pump out anywhere from three to seven articles a week. The caliber, quality and editorial perspective of those pieces waxed and waned. Some were written in haste. Some I anticipated and celebrated. Most were completely forgotten. Some, I’m sure, were never read at all.

I wrote about Trump. I wrote about solar panels, mortgages, dating apps and various Life Alert-type systems for the elderly. I wrote event guides for Los Angeles and commentary pieces about pop culture. I investigated accounting errors with the LADWP. Hell, I once ambushed a student association president with a face-to-face interview about misappropriation of funds and sweetheart no-bid deals.

Same hands. Same brain.

Wildly different amounts of intention.

I can’t say whether any of those things qualified as art. I can’t say how much of it moved the needle. I’ve had content go viral and dealt with the headaches that followed. I once attracted the attention of Jon Ronson, who marveled at our ability to publish garbage that somehow became news.

And all of this happened before generative AI gasped into existence.

Long before a chatbot could produce a passable article in seconds, the internet had already built an economy that required human beings to behave like little chatbots.

Tuesday needed content published.

Whether anyone actually had anything worth saying on Tuesday was beside the point.

More pages for Google to index. More posts for people to share. More headlines to click. More explainers. More recaps. More product comparisons. More corporate thought leadership. More episodes. More newsletters. More things filling empty slots in a CMS because an editorial calendar said those slots should not remain empty.

AI didn’t invent content without intention.

We did.

And I think that complicates the panic over what we’ve come to call AI slop.

There’s a popular chronology developing around generative AI that goes something like this:

  1. Human beings made meaningful things.

  2. Then the machines arrived.

  3. Then the slop began.

This is an appealing story. It gives us a clean before and after. It gives us something external to blame. Somewhere in the recent past lies a lost internet composed of thoughtful essays, carefully considered photographs, lovingly illustrated webpages and meaningful interpersonal exchange.

Then somebody turned on the AI image generators and ruined everything.

Come on.

We spent decades building systems designed to make humans manufacture garbage at scale.

SEO mills. Content farms. Engagement bait. Affiliate websites. Algorithmically optimized headlines. Nine-hundred-word articles answering questions that required eighty words. Corporate blogs created because somebody’s quarterly strategy deck contained the phrase thought leadership.

None of this means the people producing those things lacked creativity.

I was one of them.

Sometimes the conveyor belt produced real journalism. Sometimes it produced something funny or beautiful or genuinely useful. Sometimes somebody cared deeply about what went into the box.

Sometimes the box simply needed to be fed.

Human-made and intentional have never been synonyms.

Yet increasingly, we seem to be treating them as though they are.

Maybe that is part of what I mean by slopulism.

Not slop itself, but the belief system accumulating around it.

The conviction that our degraded cultural condition began with generative AI, and that sufficiently human production might restore whatever we believe existed before.

There is another possibility.

Maybe AI didn’t create the landfill.

Maybe it learned how to metabolize it.

I keep thinking about Back to the Future Part II.

In the first movie, Doc Brown needs something approaching a miracle to power the DeLorean. Plutonium will do it. So will a perfectly timed bolt of lightning, provided you happen to know precisely where and when it will strike.

By the second movie, there is Mr. Fusion.

Doc opens a garbage can.

A banana peel. Some leftover beer. Whatever happens to be around.

Trash goes in.

Fuel comes out.

It’s an absurd little gag about future abundance, but it increasingly feels like a useful metaphor for what happened to the internet.

For decades, we generated an unimaginable amount of cultural exhaust.

Articles. Blog posts. Government documents. Recipes. Forum arguments. Product descriptions. Fan fiction. Journalism. Academic papers. Captions. Reviews. Tutorials. Comments. Pornography. Abandoned personal websites. Corporate copy. Carefully considered essays and completely disposable horseshit.

Individually, these things had wildly different meanings and wildly different values.

Together?

Fuel.

I sometimes joke that work like mine became the Gerber baby formula of the emerging AI models. The nutrient mush that helped them take their first generative steps.

Garbage in, garbage out, they say.

Usually correctly.

But Mr. Fusion proposes that garbage might not remain garbage once something learns how to extract useful material from it.

So is generative AI a kind of recycling?

Can it take this landfill of compulsive creativity and rearrange those remnants into something worthwhile?

Can garbage become a beautiful mosaic?

Sure.

Sometimes.

It can also become shiny garbage.

So I’m not particularly interested in arguing that AI transforms trash into treasure.

We still haven’t determined whether what comes out is compost, fuel or merely a more efficiently distributed form of trash.

I wrote recently about the growing scarcity of taste.

When execution becomes abundant, I argued, the value of human contribution moves upstream.

Attention.

Intention.

Discernment.

Judgment.

Taste.

A generative system can make the image, but it can’t tell you why you needed that image.

It can produce a hundred options. Taste is what rejects ninety-nine.

It can generate the sentence. Discernment notices that the cleaner sentence is somehow less true.

The machine defaults toward the mean.

That was the argument.

But there is another question hiding inside it.

What if the mean is us?

That’s where I think the discussion of slop becomes much more uncomfortable.

Generative models were trained on the things we made.

Not merely our masterpieces.

Us.

The weird whole of us.

Our Pulitzer winners and our SEO articles about patio furniture.
Our scientific papers and our fandom arguments.
Our reporting and our marketing funnels.
Our careful sentences and our empty Tuesday content slots.

The machine doesn’t experience the hierarchy of meaning that accompanied those things when we created them.

It sees patterns.

And when those patterns are synthesized at enormous scale, perhaps what we’re seeing is something human beings have never previously had the opportunity to confront:

The visible average of our own cultural production. Or, more simply, the boring beige of humanity.

For most of the internet’s history, we encountered culture serially.

This webpage.
That article.
This photograph.
That Tumblr post.
That banner ad.
That corporate blog.
That DeviantArt drawing.

We never really stood far enough away to see the whole pile at once.

Generative AI can do something closer to that.

It compresses our accumulated conventions and hands them back to us.

The pleasant lighting.
The familiar composition.
The reassuring cadence.
The suspiciously polished whimsy.
The predictable rhetorical turn.
The cinematic image we’ve somehow seen ten thousand times without ever seeing this particular one before.

And our reaction is:

Jesus Christ. Look at this slop.

Well.
Where did it learn that?

This isn’t an argument that human culture is secretly garbage.

That would be both cynical and boring.

The average human sentence isn’t Shakespeare.

The average photograph isn’t transcendent.

The average song isn’t the song that changes your life.

Most things humans make have always been ordinary, derivative, functional, rushed, compromised, imitative, commercial or simply fine.

That’s okay.

The statistical average of human creative production should never have been confused with the boundary of human creativity.

But when an extraordinarily powerful averaging machine reproduces that center with frightening ease, we sometimes look at the result and declare that creativity itself is dying.

Maybe that’s backwards, though.

Maybe AI slop isn’t primarily a preview of our machine-made future.

Maybe it’s the first legible composite image of our human-made past.

Which would make our disgust with it a much more interesting indictment of where we’ve been than where we’re going.

The machine inherited our modularity.
Our genres.
Our formulas.
Our habits.
Our shortcuts.

Our assumptions about what a professional photograph looks like, what marketing copy sounds like, how an inspirational essay should resolve, how a movie poster should compose itself, what kind of phrase belongs on LinkedIn.

Artificial intelligence didn’t invent these conventions. It inherited them.

And then it became exceptionally good at recombining them.

That’s why so much machine output feels strangely familiar even when it depicts something nobody’s ever made before.

It’s new material assembled from old expectations.

But again, we were already doing this.

Long before any AI model could instantly generate endless streams of articles, the content economy spent twenty years telling human beings:
More.
More.
More.

Then we invented something unbelievably good at more.

And recoiled at the result.

None of this lets generative AI off the hook.

Scale changes things.

The ability to generate ten million pieces of garbage without requiring ten million bits of human labor changes things.
The economics change.
Fraud changes.
Spam changes.
Propaganda changes.

The ability to bury human communication beneath an effectively infinite supply of plausible synthetic material is not simply the content factory happening faster.

There are genuinely new problems here.

But if slop existed before the machine, then generation itself can’t be the pathology.

Something else’s gone missing.

Which brings me back to intention.

Maybe the opposite of slop isn’t human.
Maybe the opposite of slop is care.

Did somebody choose this sentence instead of merely accepting the first plausible one?

Did somebody reject twelve images because the technically prettier versions felt emotionally wrong?

Did somebody notice the strange hand?
Did somebody decide that the obvious ending was dishonest?
Did somebody have a point?

Those seem like more useful questions to me than whether a machine touched the work somewhere along the way.

Because paying a human to manually type nine hundred forgettable words about mortgage refinancing doesn’t imbue those words with spiritual value.

And using a generative system to interrogate, challenge, rearrange or visualize an idea doesn’t automatically evacuate intention from the result.

A human can be present in the production process without bringing much humanity to it.

Generative systems create an almost comical abundance of things to reject.

Which means the strange consequence of infinite production may be that the creative act moves increasingly toward refusal.

No.
Not that one.
Again.
Less polished.
More peculiar.
That sentence is smarter but this one is truer.
Remove the thing everyone expects.
Leave the mistake.
Stop.

That seems less like the death of human creativity to me than a migration of it.

The tool gets better at execution, so the human contribution shifts toward deciding what deserves to exist.

Production used to carry enough friction to impose a limit.

Now production approaches infinity and attention remains painfully finite.

Maybe taste was always quietly downstream of those economics.

Maybe we’re only now noticing because the machine finally made the imbalance impossible to ignore.

We filled the internet with everything we could make.

Now the machine can make nearly anything from what we left behind.

Maybe slopulism is what happens when we mistake our reflection for our replacement.

Author’s note

This one began as a Saturday morning brain dump: an old memory of working in content factories, a landfill metaphor, Mr. Fusion, and a nagging suspicion that maybe what we call AI slop tells us as much about the culture that trained these systems as it does about the systems themselves.

I brought that mess to ChatGPT and used it the way I increasingly prefer to use these tools: not to hand me an argument, but to push on one I was already trying to understand.

We went back and forth on the distinction between human-made and intentional, connected the idea to my earlier piece about the scarcity of taste, argued over whether the landfill became fuel, compost or simply shinier garbage, and eventually arrived at the question that became the spine of the piece: What if the mean is us?

From there, I wrote, cut, rewrote and pushed back. ChatGPT challenged places where the metaphor stopped making sense, pointed out where I was repeating an argument I’d already made elsewhere, and helped me recognize when the essay had finally found its ending.

The illustrations came from the same conversation. We developed the Sunday-comic visual language together, starting with the idea of a man outraged by what he sees in a mirror while refusing to turn around and look at the landfill behind him. I directed and iterated on the concepts; ChatGPT helped translate them into the images accompanying the piece.

Which feels appropriate.

An essay about whether AI erases human intention was made through a process in which intention was the entire point.

items.title: Baby Steps
items.description: On putting 27 billion parameters in a tiny box and immediately wanting more.
items.content:
I got Qwen3.8-27B running locally.

It felt like it was going to be a moment.

There was an intelligence in the room with me. Running silently on my Mac mini, answering my questions without reaching out to some distant data center.

It was right there. Local, untethered, open, and, if I wanted it, mine.

Here was a 2024 Mac mini (M4 Pro with 24 gigabytes of memory) quietly generating intelligence on my desk. Twenty-seven billion parameters squeezed into a box I can hold in one hand. An incredible moment by almost any reasonable standard.

My first thought was: This is incredible.

My second was: I need more RAM.

Because then I started talking to it.

The intelligence was there, certainly. It could say hello. It understood my questions and responded to them. But it wasn’t smart in the frontier-model sense. It wasn’t the level of intelligence I had (absurdly) expected to materialize inside a small aluminum box on my desk.

What an interesting kind of letdown…

A miracle happened. My expectations had simply outrun it.

Twenty-seven billion parameters isn’t a small intelligence. It only feels small because the machines that recalibrated my expectations are unimaginably large.

I’ve grown accustomed to talking with systems backed by vast data centers, armies of GPUs, and infrastructure I couldn’t begin to reproduce at home.

Then I invited one smaller intelligence into the room and wondered why it wasn’t as clever as all of them.

I blame myself. I expected a baby with a doctorate to appear.

Here was this new little mind taking its first steps, and instead of marveling at the fact that it could walk, I was disappointed it hadn’t finished its dissertation.

Still, there was something different about it.

The frontier models may be vastly more capable, but they don’t live here. I visit them. I send a message into the cloud, something enormous wakes up somewhere far away, and an answer returns. However conversational it may feel, the intelligence remains elsewhere.

This one is in the room.

I could turn off the internet and it wouldn’t disappear. I could choose the model, shape its environment, and decide when it ran. Its continued existence isn’t tied to a subscription or dependent on a company deciding I can still have access to it.

It’s not just intelligence I can use.

It’s intelligence I can keep.

That realization lasted for perhaps thirty seconds before my mind began assembling the components for a machine that might make it smarter.

Graphics cards. Cooling systems. Cables. Power supplies. A glowing Habitrail of whirring GPUs designed to give this local intelligence some room to breathe.

All of it is now painfully expensive.

I should’ve bought that RTX 5080 when I had the chance…

At the time, I thought buying one would be impulsive, so I exercised restraint. I now deeply regret that responsible decision. I could have reframed the entire purchase as an investment in sovereign intelligence.

Surely, if I give this local brain a larger playpen it could grow into something beautiful. It’ll just take more memory, more electricity, and several thousand dollars’ worth of new hardware.

What I have right now feels closer to a Tamagotchi.

It’s charming. It responds when I speak to it. I can show it to visitors and say, “Look! The rudimentary future of our digital companions lives inside this box.” Then it will confidently misunderstand something fairly basic, and we will all nod politely.

But perhaps that’s unfair.

A Tamagotchi was a simulation of something alive. This is something stranger: a real, functioning intelligence compressed down to fit inside a consumer computer, sitting silently beside me and waiting to speak.

It may not be frontier-level intelligence, but it inhabits the same physical world I do. Hell, we share the same address!

I can feel the warmth of the metal box sustaining it. I can disconnect it from everything else and it remains. I can tinker with it, constrain it, expand it, or leave it running quietly on my desk.

That feels like the beginning of something.

I can see a personal AI paradise on the horizon: private, capable intelligences that live with us, learn how we work, and answer to us rather than to the companies hosting them.

Minds we can shape without asking permission. Companions whose memories and continued existence don’t depend on a subscription staying active.

Not merely intelligence, but intimacy.

Not merely access, but ownership.

I had hoped my current hardware might take me all the way there.

It can’t.

But it did take me one step closer.

So no, I’m not disappointed.

I’m impatient.

Author’s Note

This piece began as a Saturday-morning brain dump after I got Qwen3.8-27B running on my Mac mini. The experience, excitement, disappointment, hardware envy, and questionable RTX 5080 restraint were all mine.

I brought those raw notes to Codex, and we batted the idea around together. It helped me recognize that the piece wasn’t really about disappointment. It was about impatience. And that the larger tension was between accessing intelligence somewhere else and keeping it in the room with me. From that conversation, Codex assembled a first draft. I rewrote it in my own voice, added and changed several passages, and then brought it back for a final copyedit.

The artwork followed a similar process. We developed the image of a tiny metal box casting an impossibly large shadow: the physical intelligence may be small today, but the potential it projects is nearly infinite. We explored several styles and compositions before arriving at the pulp-comic direction. Codex helped write and refine the image prompts, and I continued experimenting with them in Krea 2 Turbo.

There’s an obvious irony in using one of the frontier systems described in the essay to help articulate my feelings about a much smaller local one. But that contrast is also the point. I had the experience. I brought the taste, judgment, and final decisions. The AI helped me see more clearly what I was trying to say.

Consider this piece another small example of the future it describes.
